光學風琴屬電鳴鍵盤樂器，音色來自預錄光學音軌，以燈泡與光電二極體讀取類比波形。右: The Optigan is an electrophonic keyboard instrument whose sounds come from pre-recorded optical tracks, read by a lamp and a photodiode as analogue waveforms. The right-hand keyboard is a three-octave piano-style keyboard that plays sustained or repeating struck notes; the left-hand chord buttons control accompaniment and effects. Volume is controlled by a pedal. Its sound is limited by the optical bandwidth and by the mechanism and includes scratching and pops; the notes have no clear attack and decay. Unlike instruments that sample from magnetic tape, it uses the optical soundtrack technique of the cinema, so the sounds can grow with the discs, but the pitch changes with the speed.

The Optigan is an electronic keyboard instrument for the consumer market; it sounds from pre-recorded optical tracks: a transparent plastic film disc turns, a lamp shines through it onto a photodiode, and the analogue waveforms in concentric tracks on the disc become audio. The case is a scaled-down version of the electronic organs of the day: the three-octave keyboard at the right is played with the right hand for sustained or struck sounds, the chord buttons at the left work as on a chord organ or accordion, and rocker switches above control percussion, sound effects, introduction, fill and ending. A later version licensed for the professional market was called the Orchestron.
光學風琴的工程始於1968年，1970年取得首批專利，1971年由玩具廠商美泰兒: Work on the Optigan began in 1968; the first patents were granted in 1970, and in 1971 it was launched in El Segundo, California, by Optigan, a company under the toy firm Mattel, with the factory in Compton. It sounds from pre-recorded optical discs, an electrophone aimed at the North American consumer market; at least one television advertisement demonstrated it with the actor Carl Betz, and it appeared in the Sears–Roebuck catalogue. The version licensed for the professional market was sold as the Orchestron. In 1973 the rights, the disc format and the existing discs were resold to the New York organ maker Miner Industries, which produced it through its subsidiary Optosonic; sales rose for a time and then fell, and the instrument and discs went out of production in 1976.
演奏光學風琴時，先掀開鍵盤下方門板，將程式碟滑入氈面平台，以前緣缺口對準；關上門: To play the Optigan, first open the door under the keyboard and slide the program disc onto the felt platform, lining up the notch on its front edge; close the door and switch on, and the spindle and roller turn the disc. The right hand plays sustained or repeated struck notes on the three-octave keyboard, the left hand presses the chord buttons; the rocker switches above select percussion, sound effects, introduction, repeat sections and ending, latching up for percussion and momentary down. The thumbwheel beside the chord buttons adjusts the disc speed, which changes both tempo and pitch.

Instruments without reverb have a metal plate over the opening. The sound medium is a twelve-inch transparent plastic film disc placed on the felt platform; a white plastic cleaner is supplied, with a purple velvet-like face.
